notes.meaning: This verse opens the long story of the actual building, which runs on into the next chapters. Bezalel and Oholiab lead, and every skilled worker joins them, doing exactly what the LORD commanded. Their skill came from God. The old commentators say they worked out of love for God's service, not for money or honor.

Moses called the workers. Being gifted was not enough. They still waited for a proper call. Two things marked them out: God had given them skill, and their hearts made them willing to come. Calvin adds that even this willingness was a gift from God's Spirit.

Moses handed all the gifts to the workers and kept nothing back for himself. The building began as soon as the first gifts came in, and it never had to stop for lack of supplies. Still the people kept bringing more, every morning. Henry says giving our best to God, including prayer and praise, should be each morning's work.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic commentary Haydock calls these gifts "first-fruits," meaning the best of everything. It sees the people's eagerness as partly making up for what they had given to the golden calf.

notes.meaning: The workers stopped what they were doing and went together to tell Moses there was more than enough. The commentators praise their honesty. They could easily have kept the extra for themselves, but they refused. They did not even want to receive more than they needed, so no one could suspect them.

Moses had a message called out through the whole camp: no man or woman should make any more gifts. The people had to be held back from giving. Henry calls this rare. Most people need a push to give, but these needed a brake. By giving freely, the people showed they wanted to stay faithful to their covenant, God's binding promise with them.

From here the chapter repeats the plans of chapter 26, now reported as done. That shows the workers followed God's pattern exactly and added nothing of their own. The first piece was the inner covering: ten fine linen curtains woven with cherubim, which are winged heavenly beings. Henry sees the beautiful embroidery as a picture of the church, made lovely by the gifts of the Spirit.
Every linen curtain was cut to the same size, just as God had ordered in chapter 26. The careful measuring shows careful obedience.

The ten curtains were sewn into two large sets of five. The text keeps saying "he" did the work. That can simply mean "someone," or it may point to Bezalel as chief builder, or to each worker in turn.
Blue loops were sewn along the joining edge of each set, fifty on each side. They lined up exactly, ready to be fastened together.

Fifty gold clasps joined the two sets, so the tabernacle became one whole. Henry sees here many groups of believers joined into one church, "one Lord, one faith, one baptism." Others link it with the many parts of one body in 1 Corinthians 12.
Next came a tent of goat-hair cloth spread over the linen. There were eleven curtains, all the same size and a little longer than the linen ones. This was the outer covering of the tabernacle.
The goat-hair curtains were joined into one set of five and one set of six. Fifty loops ran along the joining edge of each set, just as in the plan.
This time the clasps were bronze, not gold. They joined the goat-hair tent into one piece.

Two more layers went on top of the goat hair: ram skins dyed red, and over them fine leather. Older translations name this top layer "badger skins" or "seal skins." Henry sees these coverings as a picture of God's shelter over his people. Whatever storms come, it does not rain in God's house.
After the coverings come the walls. Upright frames of acacia wood were made to hold up the curtains. Henry says these strong frames picture the strength of the church, even though it is only a tent.
Each frame had the same length and width, as the plan in chapter 26 required.
Each frame had two pegs, called tenons, at its foot to fit into its bases. The Pulpit Commentary says they were set evenly side by side, as in chapter 26. Every frame was made the same way.
Twenty frames formed the south wall. Under them were forty silver bases, two for each frame, one under each peg. The frames stood on silver.
The north wall matched the south wall: twenty frames on forty silver bases, two under each frame.

The back wall faced west and had six frames. Two more frames were made for the back corners. They were joined from bottom to top and held by a ring, so the corners stayed firm. The old wording "sides westward" really means the back side.
The back wall had eight frames in all, standing on sixteen silver bases, two under each frame.

Five acacia-wood crossbars were made for each of the three walls, to tie the frames together. Henry says the frames and bars locked together show how the unity of believers makes the church strong and steady.
The middle bar ran halfway up the frames, from one end of the wall to the other. It held the whole side together.
The frames and bars were covered with gold. Gold rings on the frames held the bars in place. Like the rest, this followed God's plan exactly.

Then came the veil, a large, thick curtain woven with cherubim. It hung between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place, where God's presence was. Henry and Wesley say it showed how distant God seemed in Old Testament times. The New Testament invites us to come near. It also reminds us of our life now, compared with heaven, where we will see God as he is.
The veil hung on four acacia posts covered with gold, with gold hooks. Each post stood on a silver base.

An embroidered curtain covered the entrance to the tent, between the courtyard and the Holy Place. Such curtains hung at the doors of great tents and were thought finer than wooden doors. It hung on five posts with gold-covered tops and bands, set on bronze bases. Henry says the people gathered at this door though they could not go in. In this life, we should come as near to God as we can.
